meta.blurb: Two women are found dead in a locked room in Paris, and the police are baffled. Only Auguste Dupin, a strange night-owl with a brilliant mind, can follow the clues, from a hidden window spring to a shrill voice that nobody understands.
meta.bible: Auguste Dupin: a young Parisian gentleman of good family and little money; a brilliant reasoner who loves books and night. The narrator: Dupin's unnamed friend, who shares his house and tells the story. Madame L'Espanaye: an older woman who lives quietly on the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue. Camille L'Espanaye: her daughter. Adolphe Le Bon: a young bank clerk wrongly arrested; Dupin once owed him a kindness. The Prefect of Police: the head of the Paris police, proud and unimaginative. The sailor: a tall, tanned seaman from a Maltese ship, who owns the orangutan and is innocent of the murders. The orangutan: a huge, strong ape from Borneo, brought to Paris by the sailor; it escapes with a razor. Georges Cuvier: a famous French scientist whose book describes the orangutan. Chantilly: a cobbler who became an actor, in the joke about Orion and the small man. Epicurus: an ancient Greek thinker. Orion: a group of stars. Rue Morgue: the Paris street where the crime happens. Quartier Saint-Roch: the neighbourhood. Faubourg Saint-Germain: the part of Paris where Dupin and the narrator live. Bois de Boulogne: the park where the notice says the ape was found. Jardin des Plantes: the Paris garden and zoo where the ape ends. Paris. Borneo: the island where the ape was caught. Malta. Voice and tone: a classic detective story told by the narrator; calm, clever and full of curious detail; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore. The solution: the gruff voice was the sailor's; the shrill voice was the ape's; the killer climbed up and down the lightning rod and out through a window with a hidden spring.

Dupin said that the high voice was not a human voice.

B1B2: Some people have a rare gift for solving puzzles, and they take great pleasure in it. The narrator says that this gift is not magic, but a habit of watching closely and thinking clearly.
The narrator explains that card games like whist test this gift, because a clever player notices tiny signs. A smile, a pause or a quick glance can tell him what the other players are holding.
One spring in Paris, the narrator met a young man named Auguste Dupin in a small library. They were both looking for the same rare book, and they soon began to talk.
Dupin came from a noble family, but misfortune had left him with very little money. He lived quietly on a small income and spent almost all of it on books.

The narrator offered to share a house with Dupin, and they chose an old, forgotten mansion in a quiet part of Paris. By day they closed every shutter and lived by candlelight, as if the sun did not exist.
As soon as it was dark, the two friends walked arm in arm through the busy streets of Paris. Dupin loved the lights and the crowds, and he seemed to find a story in every face.
One night they walked in silence for almost fifteen minutes. Suddenly Dupin said exactly what the narrator had been thinking, and the narrator was astonished.

Dupin explained that every thought leads to the next, like links in a chain. A fruit seller had knocked the narrator against some paving stones, and the stones had made him think of a science called stereotomy.

The narrator had looked up at the stars called Orion, and this reminded him of a cruel joke about a small man. The joke was about a shoemaker who became an actor and was laughed at for being too small, and the narrator had smiled.

A few days later, the two friends read a story in the newspaper with the title Extraordinary Murders. Early one morning, the neighbours had heard terrible screams from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue.
Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter lived alone on the fourth floor, and they hardly ever went out. They had some money saved, but they had few friends and almost no visitors.
A crowd of neighbours broke open the front door and hurried up the stairs. As they climbed, they heard two voices arguing loudly, but the voices stopped suddenly as the men reached the top.
When the men broke into the room, they found everything upside down, with broken furniture and open drawers. The younger woman had been killed, and her body was found pushed up inside the chimney.
The old woman was found dead in the small yard behind the house. Four thousand francs in gold lay untouched in the room, so the killer was clearly not a thief.
Many witnesses told the police that they had heard two voices in the house. One was deep and rough and spoke French, but the other was shrill and sounded very strange.
The witnesses could not agree about the shrill voice. One thought it was Italian, another thought it was Spanish, and another was sure it was English, but nobody could understand a word.
A surgeon who examined the bodies said that both women had been killed with enormous force. Such strength, he added, was far beyond that of any ordinary man.

The police searched every room in the house, from the cellar to the roof, but they found nobody. All the doors were locked from the inside, the windows were closed, and the chimney was far too narrow for a man.
The police arrested Adolphe Le Bon, a young bank clerk, because he had brought gold to the house three days earlier. There was no other proof against him, and he insisted that he was innocent.
Dupin said that the police had made a poor inquiry and that Le Bon had once done him a favour. He proposed that they should visit the house and look at it with their own eyes.
The two friends went to the Rue Morgue in the afternoon, and a policeman let them enter. Dupin walked slowly up and down the street and studied the front and back of the house with great care.
Inside the house, Dupin went up to the fourth floor and examined the room very slowly. He looked at the windows, the chimney and the floor, and he said almost nothing to the policemen.
On the way home, Dupin stopped at the office of a daily newspaper, and he went in alone. When he came out, he was smiling, but he did not say a word about why he had gone.

The next day at noon, Dupin asked the narrator whether he had noticed anything peculiar about the murders. He then explained that the police were confused because the crime seemed so strange, while the strangeness was actually the best guide.
Dupin pointed out something that the police had missed about the voices. Each witness had thought that the shrill voice was foreign, because it was not really speaking any language at all.
Dupin explained that the police had never really tested the windows, which seemed nailed shut. He had found a hidden spring in one of them, and a broken nail, so the window was the way out.

Near the window ran a lightning rod, a long metal pole that carries lightning to the ground. Dupin showed that no ordinary man could reach the window from the rod, so the climber must have been unusually quick and strong.

Dupin reminded him of the great strength that the crime had needed, and he gave two examples. The daughter's body had been forced far up a narrow chimney, and the mother had been thrown down from a window.
Dupin took a small tuft of hair from a pocket and showed it to the narrator. It had been found in the dead woman's grip, and it was thick, reddish-brown and clearly not human.
Dupin laid a drawing of the marks on the girl's throat on the table, and asked his friend to place his hand on it. The narrator tried, but his fingers were far too small to fit the marks.

Dupin opened a book by Cuvier, a famous scientist, and read aloud about the orangutan of the East Indian islands. The great animal, he read, was very strong and fierce, and it loved to imitate what people did.
Dupin said that the ape must belong to a sailor. He had found a ribbon near the lightning rod, tied in a knot that only sailors use.
Dupin showed the notice that he had placed in the paper the night before. It said that a large orangutan had been found in the park, and that its owner, a sailor, could claim it.
Dupin said that the sailor would probably come within the hour. He handed the narrator a pistol, but he said they would not need it, because the man was probably not a murderer.
A tall, tanned sailor stepped into the room, carrying a heavy stick. He looked strong and bold, but he was clearly nervous, and he glanced at the pistols as he said good evening.
Dupin told the sailor kindly that he knew the man was innocent of the murders. He added that he also knew the sailor had been present, and that the best thing was to tell the whole truth.
The sailor began his story with a voyage to Borneo, where he and a friend had caught a huge orangutan. The friend died, so the ape became his alone, and he took it home to Paris.
In Paris, the sailor kept the ape locked in a small room, because it was wild and dangerous. When the ape became angry, the sailor used a whip to make it obey.
One night, the ape escaped from its room and went into the sailor's bedroom. The sailor found it in front of the mirror, copying the way he shaved, with a razor in its hand.
The sailor, terrified of what the strong animal might do with the razor, held up his whip. At that, the ape escaped through a window and raced into the dark street, and the sailor ran after it.

The chase took them across the quiet city until the ape reached the Rue Morgue, at about three in the morning. There, it noticed a light and an open window on the fourth floor, and it began to climb the lightning rod.
The sailor climbed the rod as far as the window, but he could not get in. Looking into the room, he saw the ape seize Madame L'Espanaye, and the sight filled him with horror.
When the old woman screamed, the ape became frightened and angry, and in its fear it killed both women. The sailor was so horrified that he climbed down the rod and ran home without looking back.
Dupin explained that the frightened ape had tried to hide what it had done. It pushed the daughter up the chimney and threw the mother out of the window, and then it escaped down the rod.
A few days later, the sailor caught the ape himself, and he sold it for a large sum of money to the Jardin des Plantes. There it could do no harm, and Paris soon had a new animal to talk about.
The next morning, the Prefect of Police came to the house, and Dupin told him the whole story. Le Bon, the innocent clerk, was set free soon afterwards.

The Prefect was pleased that the case was over, but he was also annoyed that a private gentleman had solved it before the police. He grumbled that Dupin ought to mind his own business, and then he went away.

Dupin told his friend that the Prefect was not a stupid man, but he was too clever in small tricks to think deeply. He added that a man who looks too closely at a problem may see each part and miss the whole.
Dupin said that the truth is not always hidden deep in a well. Often it is lying on the surface, and people miss it only because they are looking for something much more difficult.

The friends returned to their quiet life of books and candlelight, and the city soon forgot the mystery of the Rue Morgue. The narrator, however, never forgot the night when his friend's clear mind turned a terrible riddle into a simple answer.
C1C2: The narrator begins by describing a rare kind of mind, the analytical mind, which takes the same delight in untangling a puzzle that a strong man takes in using his muscles. Such a person, he says, can seem almost magical to ordinary people, though his skill is only a habit of watching closely and reasoning clearly from small facts. The story that follows, he promises, will show this remarkable gift at work in the streets of Paris.

Card games such as whist, he adds, call for this gift more than chess does, because the skilled player must read the faces, the pauses and the small gestures of his opponents as carefully as he reads his own hand. A smile at the wrong moment, a hesitation before a card is laid down or the way a hand is gathered up may each betray a secret. The greatest analyst, he suggests, is the one who notices what everyone else has overlooked.

In the spring of a certain year in Paris, the narrator happened to meet a Monsieur Auguste Dupin in an obscure library, where both men were hunting for the same rare and curious book. They fell into conversation, and the narrator was soon struck by the young Frenchman's wide reading, his freshness of mind and the frank and candid way in which he spoke of his own affairs. By the end of that first long evening, the two young men felt like old friends who had been parted for years.

Dupin, the narrator learned, came from an illustrious family, but a series of misfortunes had reduced him to such poverty that he lived on a tiny income and spent nearly every coin he could spare on rare books. He needed little else, for his chief pleasures were reading, thinking and conversation, and these cost nothing at all. His imagination, the narrator found, was one of the most vivid that he had ever met.

The narrator, who could afford a little more than his friend, proposed that they share a house, and together they rented a decaying and fantastic mansion in a lonely corner of the Faubourg Saint-Germain, where no one ever called. At the first light of day they closed every heavy shutter and lit a pair of scented candles, and they passed the hours reading, writing and talking until darkness returned. Neighbours, had they known, would have thought the two young men a little mad.

As soon as night fell, the friends walked arm in arm through the crowded streets, seeking in the lights and shadows of the great city the quiet excitement that daylight could not give them. Dupin, who noticed everything, drew pleasure from the smallest signs, and he could often tell a stranger's trade, temper and troubles from a single glance. For him the whole city was a vast book that was never finished and that he never tired of reading.

One evening, after almost fifteen minutes of complete silence, Dupin remarked suddenly that the little man was too small for the part and would do better in a lighter theatre. The narrator, who had been thinking about an actor of exactly that description, felt a shock of wonder, and he demanded to know how his friend had guessed it. It seemed as though Dupin had quietly stepped into his very mind and had been sitting there all the while.

Dupin explained that he had followed his friend's thoughts link by link, as a person follows footprints across snow. A fruit seller, carrying a basket, had thrown the narrator against a heap of paving stones, and a glance at them had made him mutter a word about the cutting of stone. That word had led his mind to the old Greek thinker Epicurus, Dupin said, and from there his eyes had lifted to the night sky.

Following his friend's glance, Dupin said, he had guessed that the stars of Orion had recalled to the narrator a joke about Chantilly, a poor shoemaker who had tried to become a tragic actor. The narrator had smiled, then drawn himself up to his full height, and Dupin had read in that movement the thought that the little man was too small for serious parts. The narrator, amazed, could only admit that every link in the long chain was exactly true, and he was a little frightened by such skill.

Soon afterwards, the friends were reading the morning paper when their eyes fell on a long article headed Extraordinary Murders, which described a crime so strange that all of Paris was talking of it. At about three o'clock one morning, the paper said, the people of the Quartier Saint-Roch had been woken by a series of terrible screams coming from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue. The house was the home of a Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter Camille, two quiet women whom the neighbours knew only by sight.

The two ladies, according to the paper, had lived there for several years in complete retirement, seeing almost no one and going out only on the rarest occasions. They were thought to have some money put by, and they employed no servant, and nobody in the neighbourhood could say that they had an enemy. Nothing in their quiet lives, said the neighbours, could explain what had happened that night.

A crowd of neighbours, alarmed by the screams, forced the front door with an iron bar and hurried up the staircase together, though they were afraid of what they might find. As they climbed, they heard two voices in angry dispute, one gruff and one thin and shrill, but when they reached the first landing the sounds stopped completely, and the house fell silent. Every room they entered seemed empty, until at last they came to the locked door of a chamber at the back of the house.

When the men broke into the room, they found it in the wildest disorder, with furniture smashed, the bed torn from its place, the drawers pulled open and a razor lying on one of the chairs. Mademoiselle Camille L'Espanaye lay dead, and her body had been forced up the chimney, so that only with great effort could the men draw it down. Of her mother there was no sign in the room, and the neighbours looked around in growing horror.

Madame L'Espanaye was found at last in the small paved yard behind the house, lifeless and so badly hurt by what had been done to her that the neighbours could hardly look. In the room above, on the other hand, bags holding four thousand francs in gold still lay on the floor, and the drawers contained jewels and silver that no robber had touched. Whatever the murderer had come for, it was plainly not for money, and that fact made the crime stranger still.

At the inquiry, many neighbours agreed on one point, that they had heard two voices quarrelling at the top of the house, and they agreed too that the first was a deep, rough voice speaking French. The second, which was higher and sharper, puzzled everyone, because it was more like a shriek than the sound of words, and nobody could tell what it said. Every witness, however, was certain that it did not belong to either of the dead women.

Strangely, every witness who had heard the shrill voice believed it to be the speech of some foreign country. They all named a different land: one man said Spanish, another Italian, a third German, and a fourth was certain that it was Russian, although none of them knew those languages well. It seemed that the sound belonged to no nation on earth, and the police found the fact deeply puzzling.

The surgeon who examined the bodies reported that both women had been killed with a violence far beyond what he had ever seen, and that an ordinary man could scarcely have shown such strength. The younger woman, he said, had been strangled, and the older one had suffered injuries so severe that she could not have survived them for a moment. The police listened gravely and wrote down every word, but they could not make sense of any of it.

The police examined every corner of the house, from the cellars to the roof, and they even searched the chimneys with long poles, yet they found no trace of anyone who might have done the deed. The door of the room had been locked on the inside, the key still standing in the lock, and both windows were firmly fastened from within. The narrow chimney could not have let a grown man pass, and the baffled officers declared that the murderer must have vanished into the air.

In their search for a culprit, the police arrested Adolphe Le Bon, a young clerk at a bank, who had carried a sum of gold to Madame L'Espanaye's house three days before the crime. There was no evidence against him except that fact, and he protested again and again that he knew nothing of the matter, but the officials felt they had to arrest someone. Le Bon was locked in prison, and the story of the crime ended there in the papers, leaving every thoughtful reader unsatisfied.

Dupin, who had no opinion of the police, declared that their inquiry was clumsy and shortsighted, and he reminded his friend that Le Bon had once done him a kindness. He proposed that they should investigate the crime for themselves, as a form of entertainment, and obtained permission from the Prefect of Police to examine the house. The narrator, who had never seen his friend so eager, was fascinated and agreed at once to go with him.

That afternoon the two friends went to the Rue Morgue, where a crowd still lingered in front of the house and a policeman stood on guard at the door. Dupin, instead of hurrying inside, walked slowly up and down the street, then circled the building and studied the doors, the windows and the neighbouring houses with a care that astonished his companion. At last he showed the permission he had obtained, and the two friends were allowed to go inside.

Inside the house, Dupin climbed to the fourth floor and examined the fatal room with slow, silent attention, passing from the windows to the chimney and from the chimney to the floor. The narrator followed him in bewilderment, while Dupin asked the officer on duty a few brief questions and made no comment on the answers. By the time he had finished, the daylight was nearly gone, and the two friends walked home through the darkening streets.

On the way home, Dupin stopped at the office of one of the daily newspapers and went in alone, leaving the narrator to wait in the street and wonder what business his friend could have there. When he came out a few minutes later, he was smiling quietly, but he said nothing whatever of his errand. All that evening he was in the best of humours, and he talked of everything except the murders.

The next day at noon, Dupin asked the narrator whether he had noticed anything peculiar about the murders, and, when the answer was a puzzled no, he began to explain his own method. The police, he said, were bewildered precisely because the crime seemed so strange, whereas an unusual feature, far from hiding the truth, is the thread that leads to it. A reasoner should ask not what has happened, but what has happened that has never happened before.

Dupin pointed out that the police had overlooked the real meaning of the witnesses' evidence: several people, from different countries, had called the shrill voice foreign, and yet not one of them had understood a single word of it. A voice that every nation thought foreign, he argued, might well be one that belonged to no nation, and perhaps to no human being at all. The idea was so strange that the narrator could only stare at him in silence for some moments.

Dupin then explained that the police had never really tested the windows, which seemed to be firmly nailed from within. In one frame he had found a hidden spring and a nail broken through, so that the window had fastened itself again after the murderer left, and the killer had clearly gone out that way. The locked room, he said, was an illusion, and the only question was how anyone could have reached the window, which was a long way from the ground.

Close to the window stood a lightning rod, and from it a shutter hung open, but Dupin showed by careful measurement that no ordinary man could cross the gap between the rod and the window without help of some kind. It would need a creature of astonishing agility, he said, one that could climb a bare pole and swing across to the sill with perfect confidence. The narrator, listening intently, was beginning to feel the hair rise on the back of his neck.

Dupin next drew attention to the astonishing strength that the crime had demanded, since the younger woman's body had been forced far up a chimney so narrow that several men had struggled to drag it down. The older woman, moreover, had been thrown from the fourth-floor window into the yard with a force that no ordinary man could have used. Strength like that, he added, belonged less to a human being than to a wild beast.

Dupin took from his pocket a small tuft of coarse tawny hair which he had found, tightly gripped, in the dead woman's hand. He explained that it was not human hair, for human hair is much finer, and that the narrator should note how it differed from anything he had seen on a man's head. Here, it seemed, was the first real clue to the shrill voice and the superhuman strength.

Next, Dupin spread out a sheet of paper on which he had carefully drawn the marks left on the daughter's throat, and he invited the narrator to place his own hand upon them, finger for finger. The narrator tried again and again, but his fingers were far too short and too close together, and he could not match the wide, strong shape that the marks revealed. No human hand, Dupin said in a quiet and certain voice, had ever made such marks as those.

Opening a volume by the great scientist Cuvier, Dupin read aloud a description of the large orangutan of the East Indian islands, whose gigantic size, prodigious strength and activity, wild ferocity and love of imitation are well known to naturalists. When he had finished, the narrator understood at last, with a mixture of horror and relief, that the shrill voice, the tawny hair and the enormous hand all pointed to one creature. Everything fitted, except for the one fact that no one had imagined: that such an animal could be loose in the middle of Paris.

Dupin added that the ape's owner was almost certainly a sailor, for at the foot of the lightning rod he had picked up a greasy scrap of ribbon. It was tied in a knot that is used only by sailors, and especially by those who sail from Malta, and it had clearly been used to tie back a seaman's long hair. The man who owned that ribbon, Dupin reasoned, could not be the murderer, and he must be terribly worried about his missing animal, so he had taken a step to bring him forward.

Dupin handed him the newspaper, and the narrator read an advertisement saying that a large tawny orangutan of the Borneo kind had been caught in a park early on the morning of the murders. Its owner, who was known to be a sailor from a Maltese ship, might have it back by describing it correctly and paying a small sum for its keep. Dupin explained, with a quiet smile, that he had set this gentle trap because he knew the sailor would be too anxious about his pet to stay away.

Dupin said that the sailor would probably arrive within the hour, and he handed the narrator a pistol, taking another himself, though he did not think that they would need to use them. The two friends sat quietly in the candlelit room, the narrator unable to guess how a stranger could be so certain to appear. Footsteps soon sounded on the stairs, slow and uncertain, and then a knock came at the door.

The visitor proved to be a tall, powerfully built sailor, with a sunburnt face and a heavy cudgel in his hand, who had the look of a man who feared nothing in the world except what he had come about. He bowed clumsily, spoke in a rough voice, and asked politely whether he might see the orangutan. Dupin, who had quietly locked the door while the man was speaking, invited him to sit down.

Dupin told the sailor, in a gentle and reassuring tone, that he and his friend meant him no harm, and that they knew perfectly well that he had no hand in the murders. At the same time, he said, the man had certainly been present, and he must understand that an innocent person, Le Bon, was at that moment in prison for a crime that he had not committed. The sailor, who had begun by looking ready to fight, sank back in his chair, and his rough face went white.

The sailor, speaking with growing ease, said that he had gone on a voyage to the East Indian islands, where he and a companion had captured a great orangutan in the forests of Borneo. When the companion died, the animal became his alone, and after a difficult journey, in which its fierce temper caused him constant trouble, he brought it home to Paris. He had planned to sell it for a large sum of money, once its temper had been tamed.

In Paris the sailor, who hoped to sell the animal quietly and who did not want the neighbours to know about it, kept the orangutan locked in a small room at the back of his lodging. Whenever the creature grew angry or unruly, he used a whip to make it obey, and in this way he had been able to control it, though he never entirely trusted it. The ape, for its part, watched its master closely and learned all of his habits, and it forgot nothing.

One night, however, the animal escaped from its room and made its way to the sailor's bedroom, where he found it before a looking-glass, razor in hand and face covered with soap. It was copying, with great seriousness, the way in which it had so often seen its master shave, and the sight froze the sailor in the doorway. For a moment he did not dare to move, and then, remembering the whip, he took a step forward.

The sailor, terrified of what such a powerful creature might do with a razor, raised his whip, and the ape sprang through the door and fled through a window into the street. It ran off with the razor still in its hand, stopping now and then to glance back at its master. The sailor, half dressed and half mad with fear, ran after it through the empty streets of the sleeping city.

The chase led across the sleeping city until, at about three in the morning, the ape turned into the Rue Morgue, where the light of a candle at an open window on the fourth floor caught its attention. With a speed that astonished the breathless sailor, it climbed the lightning rod, caught hold of the shutter, swung itself across, and sprang into the room. The sailor, unable to follow so easily, stopped in the street below, wondering what he should do.

The sailor, an active man, climbed the rod as far as the level of the window, but he could go no farther, and so he clung there and looked into the room. He saw the two women, who had been sitting up late with their papers, rise in terror, and he saw the ape seize Madame L'Espanaye by the hair and flourish the razor near her face. Her screams, he knew, would soon bring the whole street out of bed, and his own heart was pounding with dread.

When the old woman struggled and screamed, the animal, afraid of being punished for its escape, grew furious, and what followed was so terrible that the sailor could hardly speak of it afterwards. Sick with horror, he cried out in a hoarse voice, slid down the rod and ran home as fast as his legs would carry him, determined to know nothing of the matter. That cry, Dupin pointed out, was the gruff French voice that the neighbours had heard from the stairs.

Dupin explained that the ape, afraid of the punishment it expected, had tried to hide its work by forcing the younger woman's body up the chimney and throwing the older woman from the window. It had then swung back to the lightning rod and slid down it, vanishing into the darkness before the neighbours broke into the room. The locked door, the open window and the shrill, wordless voice were all explained at last, and no ghost was needed.

Some days later, the sailor managed to catch the runaway himself, and he sold it for a very large sum to the Jardin des Plantes, the famous garden and menagerie of Paris. There the great animal lived behind strong bars, where it could do no harm, and thousands of curious visitors came to look at the creature that had puzzled the finest minds in the city. The sailor, for his part, was glad to be rid of the creature, and still gladder that nobody blamed him for what it had done.

The following morning, the Prefect of Police called at the house, curious to learn what the two friends had been doing, and Dupin told him the whole story from beginning to end, laying out each clue in its proper order. The Prefect, startled but too sensible to doubt the evidence, gave orders at once for the release of Le Bon. The poor clerk walked out of prison a free man and went back to his work at the bank.

The Prefect, however, was not entirely pleased, for he disliked being beaten at his own work by a private gentleman, and he muttered a few sharp words about people who meddled. Dupin merely smiled, offered him a chair and let him grumble, since he knew that the poor man had done his best according to his own lights. When the officer had gone, the two friends sat together in the silence of the shuttered room.

Dupin remarked, with a gentle shrug, that the Prefect was too cunning to be profound, for he saw every small detail but never the shape of the thing as a whole. A man who stares too closely at a single star, he explained, may lose it altogether, while a glance slightly to one side shows it brightly. In the same way the strangeness of the crime, which had baffled the police, had been the very light that guided him to the answer.

The truth, Dupin said, is not always at the bottom of a well, but is often found on the surface of things, where careless eyes pass over it because it looks too simple. He reminded his friend that his own success had come not from deep learning but from patient observation and from a willingness to believe the unbelievable when the evidence required it. The narrator, who had watched the whole case unfold from his chair, could only bow his head in agreement.

The two friends returned to their quiet life of books, candlelight and midnight walks, and Paris, which never stays long on one subject, soon forgot the horror of the Rue Morgue. The narrator, however, never forgot how a crime that had seemed beyond the power of reason had been solved by a single patient mind, and how an orangutan had been the strangest murderer in the history of the city. He would always remember that summer as the one in which he saw a friend's gift at its brightest.
